\chapter{Day}
\label{ch:ka-day}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} in Kannada and tell it apart from the native word for daytime.}

Say \kn{ದಿನ}, kept whole as a Sanskrit tatsama where Hindi's din eroded, and set it against native \kn{ಹಗಲು}, which means daytime rather than a day.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dina]{\kn{ದಿನ} (dina) — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit kept whole}

\label{lesson:KA-C23-dina}



\begin{quote}
You've already met Sanskrit's \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{} compounds for noon and midnight. Here's the plain word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} itself — and a genuinely interesting twist on how borrowing works.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\kn{ದಿನ}} (\textbf{dina}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} — is a Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama} word: borrowed \textbf{whole}, unchanged, the same way \emph{madhyāhna}/\emph{madhyarātri} were (Chapter 17). It's Kannada's ordinary, everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}a day.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here's the honest twist: Kannada's \emph{dina} and Hindi's \textbf{\dv{दिन}} (\emph{din}) trace to the \textbf{exact same} Sanskrit word, \textbf{\dv{दिन}} (\emph{dina}) — but they got there by \textbf{different routes}. Hindi's \emph{din} is a \textbf{tadbhava} form: Sanskrit \emph{dina} wore down naturally over centuries, through Prakrit, losing its final vowel along the way. Kannada's \emph{dina}, by contrast, is a direct \textbf{tatsama} borrowing — taken straight from Sanskrit, unworn, keeping the full shape. So Kannada's \emph{dina} and Hindi's \emph{din} look almost identical, but one is an unbroken \textbf{inheritance} (eroded), the other a \textbf{later borrowing} (kept whole) — genuinely different histories landing on nearly the same modern word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Kannada does have a genuine \textbf{native Dravidian} word here too: \textbf{\kn{ಹಗಲು}} (\emph{hagalu}) — but be careful, it means specifically \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{daytime}\textquotedblright{} (the daylight hours, as opposed to night), not \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a day}\textquotedblright{} as a calendar unit. It's not a synonym for \emph{dina}; it's a different sense of \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dina\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} Sanskrit tatsama, kept whole
  \item the twist — dina and Hindi's din, same Sanskrit source, but borrowing vs. natural erosion
  \item hagalu — native Dravidian, \textquotedblleft{}daytime,\textquotedblright{} a different sense than dina
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is Kannada's \textbf{\kn{ದಿನ}} a tatsama borrowing or a tadbhava inheritance? (\textbf{Tatsama} — borrowed whole from Sanskrit.) How does this differ from Hindi's \textbf{\dv{दिन}} (\emph{din}), even though both trace to the same Sanskrit word? (\textbf{Din is tadbhava} — naturally eroded through Prakrit — while Kannada's \emph{dina} was borrowed later, unworn.) What does \textbf{\kn{ಹಗಲು}} (\emph{hagalu}) mean, and is it a synonym for \emph{dina}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Daytime\textquotedblright{}} — a different sense, not \textquotedblleft{}a day\textquotedblright{} as a calendar unit.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\kn{ಊ} — one character, the long partner of one you already have}

\label{lesson:KA-S127-letter-uu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಉ} — what sound does it carry, and does it stand alone or ride on a consonant?

One character this time. It is the same vowel held longer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಊ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಊ}} — \emph{ū}, the long \emph{u}.

Kannada keeps \textbf{short and long as two different letters}, not as one letter with a mark on it. So the vowel you met two chapters ago has a partner:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಉ}} — \emph{u}, short. Say it and stop.
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} — \emph{ū}, long. Say it and hold it about twice as long.
\end{itemize}

Look at the shapes: \textbf{\kn{ಊ}} is \textbf{\kn{ಉ}} with an extra stroke. Kannada builds the long vowel out of the short one and repeats that habit across its vowels.

The length is not decoration. It separates words, the way \emph{ship} and \emph{sheep} are separated by nothing else.

\textbf{\kn{ಊ}} has a riding half too. You have already read it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಮೂರು}} \emph{mūru} — three
\end{itemize}

That \textbf{\kn{ೂ}} in the middle is this same long vowel, drawn as a tail on \textbf{\kn{ಮ}}. Take the consonant away and it has to stand up, and standing up it is \textbf{\kn{ಊ}}.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಊ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಊ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two and say which is the long one
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಉ}  ·  \kn{ಊ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಊ} three times, holding the \emph{ū} long as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} at \kn{ಮೂರು} and find the riding half of today's letter inside it
  \item \emph{Say it:} the short one, then the long one — \textquotedblleft{}u … ū\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಊ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ū}}, the long \emph{u}.) How is its shape related to \kn{ಉ}? (It is \kn{ಉ} with an added stroke.) What is its riding half, and in which word have you already read it? (\textbf{\kn{ೂ}}, in \emph{mūru}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
